name: K'iche'
variety: Western and central K'iche' of the Nahualá and Totonicapán type, which keeps five short and five long vowels; dialects such as Cantel and Chichicastenango have turned the length contrast into a tense and lax contrast. eSpeak NG reads the ALMG-based spelling
sources: Larsen, Thomas W. (1988). Manifestations of Ergativity in Quiché Grammar. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley.
Mondloch, James L. (1978). Basic Quiché Grammar. Albany: Institute for Mesoamerican Studies, State University of New York.
López Ixcoy, Candelaria Dominga (1997). Ri Ukemiik ri K'ichee' Chii': Gramática K'ichee'. Guatemala: Cholsamaj.
Bennett, Ryan (2016). Mayan phonology. Language and Linguistics Compass 10(10), 469-514.
England, Nora C. & Baird, Brandon O. (2017). Phonology and phonetics. In J. Aissen, N. C. England & R. Zavala Maldonado (eds.), The Mayan Languages. London: Routledge.

Pinkerton, Sandra (1986). Quichean (Mayan) glottalized and nonglottalized stops: a phonetic study with implications for phonological universals. In J. J. Ohala & J. J. Jaeger (eds.), Experimental Phonology. Orlando: Academic Press.
Nielsen, Kuniko (2005). Kiche intonation. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 104, 45-60.
Baird, Brandon O. (2014). An Acoustic Analysis of Contrastive Focus Marking in Spanish-K'ichee' (Mayan) Bilingual Intonation. PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Austin.
Wood, Elizabeth Anne (2025). An acoustic study of tense, lax, and glottalized vowels in Chichicastenango K'iche' (Maya). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 55(3), 398-434.
contrasts: plain versus glottalised stops and affricates at six places: p and ɓ, t and tʼ, ts and tsʼ, tʃ and tʃʼ, k and kʼ, q and qʼ
the glottalised labial is a voiced implosive, the others are ejectives

short versus long vowels in the conservative dialects (chaj 'pine' versus chaaj 'ash', written chäj and chaj in the spelling that marks lax vowels); tense versus lax vowels, or six vowels without length, in the innovating dialects
glottal stop as a consonant, also after vowels (V'C)
no voiced stops apart from the implosive
allophony: plain stops and affricates are aspirated at the end of a word and before another consonant, and unaspirated before a vowel
/ɓ/ is a weak voiced implosive; at the end of a word it is devoiced or glottalised without voicing
/qʼ/ is often a voiceless uvular implosive rather than an ejective, and /tʼ/ varies between ejective and implosive (Pinkerton 1986)
/l r w j/ are devoiced and fricated at the end of a word and before voiceless consonants: [ɬ], voiceless r, [ʍ] or [ɸ], [ç]
/r/ varies between a tap and a trill
/χ/ (written j) ranges from uvular to velar [x]
short vowels are lax and centralised, short /a/ towards [ə]; unstressed short vowels are reduced or dropped, above all in the syllable before the stressed one
a vowel before a glottal stop is creaky or interrupted; full closure is rare (Wood 2025)
ejectives and the glottal stop raise the pitch of the preceding vowel (Nielsen 2005)
syllable_structure: CV(ː)C as the basic root shape; CV, CVC, CVːC, CVʔC, with onset clusters CCVC through prefixes and vowel loss
phonotactics: roots are mostly CVC; words end in a consonant more often than in a vowel
onset clusters arise when an unstressed vowel is lost (penultimate syncope); coda clusters are rare except with a glottal stop as first member
m, n, l, r may be syllabic
long vowels occur mainly in stressed final syllables

stress.rule: Stress falls on the last syllable of the word; following clitics do not take it; recent Spanish loans may keep penultimate stress (mango, plato).
stress.cues: a rise in pitch on the stressed syllable is the main cue; duration adds to it in dialects without a length contrast (Cantel) but not in Nahualá; intensity

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong: unstressed short vowels are centralised or deleted
rhythm.notes: No rhythm metrics are published to my knowledge. Reduction and loss of unstressed vowels and the resulting clusters point towards stress timing; the final lengthening value is a default.

length.notes: In Chichicastenango, where the old long and short vowels are now tense and lax, tense vowels average 144 ms, lax vowels are about 20 ms shorter and glottalised vowels about 34 ms longer (Wood 2025). Comparable figures for a dialect with a plain length contrast were not available to me.

intonation.declarative: each content word forms an accentual phrase with a rise (LH*) on its stressed final syllable; the pitch stays high to the end of the phrase; the utterance ends in a fall to low (L-L%) that overrides the last accent
intonation.yes_no_question: begins with the question particle (l)a on a very low pitch, has a reduced pitch range in the middle and ends in a rise to the top of the speaker's range (H-H%, about 200 Hz for the male speaker of Nielsen 2005)
intonation.wh_question: ends in a fall (L-L%), like statements
intonation.continuation: intermediate phrases end high (H-); tag questions and some imperatives end on a mid-high plateau (H-L%)
intonation.accent_shape: LH*: low at the start of the stressed final syllable, rising to a peak at its end
intonation.notes: After Nielsen (2005), based on one speaker of West Central K'iche'.

tone.notes: K'iche' has no lexical tone; pitch marks stress and phrasing.

phonation: ejective stops and affricates tʼ tsʼ tʃʼ kʼ qʼ
implosive ɓ, and implosive variants of qʼ and tʼ
creaky or interrupted vowels before a glottal stop

problems: the phoneme table quc is declared without a phoneme file of its own, so the language uses the generic base vowels and consonants
glottalised consonants are rendered as a glottal stop followed by a plain stop ([ʔk], [ʔq], [ʔt], [ʔb], [ʔtʃ]); there are no ejective or implosive phonemes
tz' and ch' fail at the start of a word: tz'i' and ch'ich' are partly spelled out as English letter names; inside a word tz' comes out as a glottal stop plus t plus voiced [z]
an apostrophe at the end of a word is dropped and replaced by a pause, so final b', k', q' and the final glottal stop (che') lose their glottalisation
o is pronounced as the two vowels o and u (job' has two syllables) and u is always long; the rules for these two letters do not match any description of the language
vowel length is not handled: double vowels become two syllables, and the diaeresis letters ä ë ï ö ü for lax vowels are replaced by the plain vowels
w is [v] and j is [h]; the literature has [w] with a devoiced or fricated final variant, and a uvular or velar fricative
no aspiration of final stops, no devoicing of final sonorants, no reduction of unstressed vowels in the phoneme table (the voice file only lowers their amplitude and length)
the number words in the word list are typed in spelling but read as phoneme codes, so jun is said with [j]; numbers above ten are read digit by digit
good: a uvular stop q distinct from k
x as [ʃ], tz as [ts], ch as [tʃ]

notes: Baird's work and Wood (2025) report vowel formants as plots or normalised values; I found no table of raw formant values and give no formant block.
